title: Amazing Game!! 95% Accuracy! | Grunfeld Defense | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We open with the queen's pawn, looking for a solid, structured game.
The fianchetto — this could be a King's Indian or a Grünfeld.

Black commits to the Grünfeld with d5 — the ultimate hypermodern opening. It concedes the center on purpose, then swarms it with pieces. You rarely see it below master level because it demands staggering memorization; it's one of the hardest openings to learn.
teaches: the Grünfeld hypermodern idea

moves.spoken: The natural e4 kicks the knight and builds the broad pawn center Black has invited us to build.

There's the hypermodern bargain: Black lets us plant pawns on d4 and c3 and fianchettoes, planning to strike with c5, the knight to c6, and the bishop to g4 — giving up the center only to assault it as fast as possible.
teaches: Black concedes then attacks the center

moves.spoken: Here's my sideline that sidesteps the theoretical ocean — the bishop check on b5. Practically it's hard for Black to equalize against it.
teaches: a practical anti-Grünfeld sideline

moves.spoken: The point is simpler than it looks: induce c6, then tuck the bishop back to a4. It delays Black's freeing c5, slices through the position, and can later drop to b3 to eye f7.
teaches: induce c6 to delay c5

moves.spoken: The knight goes to e2, not f3 — f3 would walk into the g4 pin, while e2 keeps f3 in reserve to shoo the bishop and, above all, lends another defender to the d4-pawn for the coming c5 and Nc6 pressure.
teaches: Ne2 keeps f3 available and guards d4

moves.spoken: Black hits the center the classical way with c5. No action needed yet: the d4-pawn is defended three times and attacked three — no fourth defender required until it is.
teaches: count attackers and defenders before reacting

moves.spoken: Top priority is getting the king out of the center, so we castle. A brazen h4 lunge would be far too loose with our center already under fire.

Black develops to c6, and it's tempting to swap it off — but capturing wrecks our light squares: it opens the bishop's path to a6 to harass the e2-knight, and the doubled c-pawns actually become a Grünfeld asset. So we don't take.
teaches: why Bxc6 helps Black

moves.spoken: Instead we bring up reinforcements — the bishop to e3, buttressing d4. White is now a shade better.
The bishop to d7 is passive; it's fair to say White already holds a pleasant edge out of the opening.

Now a plan: lift the rook off a1 so a future d5 never drops it, and Rc1 reads better than Rb1, which would hand Black an anchor on a5. One caution — with the bishops eyeing each other, always watch for a knight-takes-d4 trick, which only bites once the queen loses contact with its bishop.
teaches: unpin before the d5 break
beware Nxd4 when the bishops face off

moves.spoken: A mysterious but strong improving move — the rook to c5. It's hard to evict, it prepares d5, and it isn't committal: a lifted piece can always come back down.
teaches: a rook lift that isn’t committal

moves.spoken: We keep the bishops on with the retreat to b3, backing the future d5 break rather than trading pieces.
With the rooks traded the queen finally comes to d2, connecting our forces free of any Nxd4 tricks.
An instructive rook choice: not c1, which becomes a veiled trade once Black answers with his own rook, but the rook to d1 — the side with the space advantage wants to keep pieces on.
teaches: the space side keeps pieces on

moves.spoken: f3 shores up the e4-pawn and locks the little chain together.

The classic h4. Not a three-move mate — a nagging, Soviet-style improving move that leans on Black's g6 hook. We march to h5 and maybe h6 to seed back-rank ideas; our king is perfectly safe and Black has no counterplay at all.
teaches: h4 exploits the g6 hook

moves.spoken: Black replies h5, softening the dark squares his fianchetto bishop was covering even further.
So the bishop swings to h6 to trade off that Grünfeld bishop and multiply the kingside weaknesses — that bishop's old job of holding d4 is now taken over by the e2-knight.
teaches: trade the fianchetto bishop, keep d4 held

moves.spoken: This trade is a limited-time offer: taking on g7 lets us plant the knight on f4 — impossible right now, since it would sever queen and bishop and hang the h6-bishop.
teaches: sequence the captures to keep the pieces connected

moves.spoken: The decision: the knight to g3, playing for mate. Unlike f4 it keeps the queen's road to g5 open, setting up the jump to h5.
teaches: choose the square that keeps the attack flowing

moves.spoken: We dive in with the queen to g5, eyeing h5. A sac on h5 right now would be two empty checks — no pieces behind it — so we build first.
teaches: don’t sacrifice without follow-up force

moves.spoken: With the king on h7 the d5 break opens a second front: after d5 the g3-knight gets the e4 and f6 route, and the b3-bishop can drop to c2 to reinforce the threat on h5.
plans: d5 to open a second front
Ne4-f6 and Bc2 to pile on h5

moves.spoken: d5 — opening the center is all in our favor here; it carries the strong points of e5 with none of the drawbacks, and it threatens to take on e6.
We recapture with the e-pawn, not the bishop, which would leave the d1-rook loose. This keeps a passed pawn rolling toward d6 and opens both the knight's and the bishop's pathways.
teaches: recapture to keep the passer and the lines

moves.spoken: f5 reeks of desperation but has a point — trying to stop the knight reaching e4 and to hem in our light-squared bishop.
Back to the trump card: push d6. It reopens the fire on the d8-rook, and a tactic is already brewing off exactly that.
The deflection: the bishop to f7 hits g6 and forces the queen to take, or it's mate — after which we grab the rook and the pawn queens.
teaches: deflection to the promotion

moves.spoken: We collect the rook. The rest is just clean technique.
Don't grab with the queen — win as simply as possible, the discipline that matters once you're winning.
teaches: simplest, not flashiest, when ahead

moves.spoken: The simplest path is to push d7, threatening to promote — no need to trade queens at all.
Simpler still: step the queen off d8 so that promoting is unstoppable, and if the knight is given up we recapture and win the queen anyway.
The finishing shot is the rook taking on d5, and after the queen recaptures the promotion arrives with a discovered check.
teaches: clear the path so promotion comes with check

moves.spoken: We promote to a knight with check — the underpromotion delivers a discovered check on the king, winning the queen and the game.
teaches: promotion-with-check underpromotion

moves.spoken: The key contrast: in the King's Indian Black plays the bishop out early and lets White build a huge pawn front, planning a slow kingside pawn storm.
teaches: King’s Indian vs Grünfeld

moves.spoken: In the King's Indian White usually locks the center with d5, producing a closed position and opposite-wing attacks — White on the queenside, Black on the kingside.
teaches: the closed KID with opposite-side attacks

moves.spoken: The Grünfeld is a different animal: Black not only concedes the center but pries it open, so the tactics arrive far earlier — frontloaded into the opening rather than saved for the middlegame like in the King's Indian.
teaches: Grünfeld tactics come early

moves.spoken: Taking on d5 is not forced. One of the most popular modern setups is a London-style treatment: the knight to f3 and the bishop to f4.
And Black answers with c5, the super-typical Grünfeld pawn lever against that structure.
teaches: the c5 lever

moves.spoken: Another topical try is the Russian System with the queen to b3, angling to make Black be the one to release the tension on c4.

A trap worth knowing: capturing on d5 with the pawn is the mistake — the knight recapture is correct, because the queen on a5 pins the c3-knight, so after the queen takes on d5 the bishop check on c3 wins material.
teaches: the Qa5 pin and Bxc3+ shot

moves.spoken: So the main line runs with the queen to a4; Black recaptures on c5, White chases with the queen to b5, and the resulting endgame is known to be equal.
